title: Parcel Mega-Hub
subtitle: Your online order's six-minute journey through a sorting centre
summary: Trucks unload at one end, cross-belt carriages tip parcels down chutes, robots carry shelves to pack stations and outbound trucks load at the other — the hub is a queueing machine with a bottleneck that moves.
overview: A parcel mega-hub is the place where thousands of individually addressed boxes become a sorted stream. Trailers back onto the inbound doors, telescopic conveyors reach inside, and every parcel is scanned, weighed and singulated — spaced exactly one carriage apart — before it is allowed onto the sorter.

The heart is the cross-belt sorter: an endless loop of carriages, each carrying a short belt that can tip left or right. The control system knows the destination of every parcel and, at the exact moment a carriage passes the right chute, the belt fires and the parcel slides down into a bag, cage or roll container. A big sorter can do 40,000 parcels an hour at 2.5 m/s, and every chute must keep up.

Around the sorter, a second swarm does the picking: low AMR robots drive under shelving pods, lift them and carry them to pack stations, so a picker never walks an aisle. At peak — the weeks before a holiday — the inflow can double while the sorter's speed cannot, and the backlog becomes the number that everyone watches.

controls.label: Parcels arriving
controls.help: The inbound stream. Every stage downstream must keep up with it.

controls.label: Sorter speed
controls.help: Faster moves more parcels, but the tilt window shrinks and jams get likelier.

controls.label: AMR fleet
controls.help: Robots feed induction and picking. Too few and the sorter starves.

steps.title: The six-minute promise
body: Inside a hub a parcel is never still for long. It is unloaded, scanned, spaced, sorted, bagged and loaded again in minutes — and every one of those moves is planned so that the sorter never has an empty slot and never gets two parcels at once.

The machine you see here is a queueing system: each stage has a maximum rate, and the slowest stage sets the tempo. Change the controls and watch the bottleneck move from the induct to the sorter, the chutes or the robots.

steps.title: Unloading the trailer
body: Trailers are packed floor to ceiling. A telescopic conveyor reaches deep into the trailer and two loaders place parcels on it as fast as they can read the labels; a scanner above the belt reads every barcode and a camera records the six faces of the box.

The first rule of a hub is singulation: parcels must arrive on the main belt one at a time, with a gap between them. Two parcels touching at the induct become one parcel for the sorter, and one of them is going to the wrong place.

steps.title: Induct and scan
body: At the induct station an operator — or a robot arm — places each parcel on the belt at a fixed pitch. The scanner reads the address, looks up the destination chute, and the hub's control system reserves a carriage on the sorter for that parcel.

Push the arrival rate to 60,000 parcels an hour and watch the induction stage become the limit: the fleet cannot feed the belt any faster, so the sorter runs below capacity even though it could take more.

steps.title: The cross-belt sorter
body: Each carriage carries a short belt across its top. When the carriage reaches the chute for its parcel, the belt motors run for a fraction of a second and throw the parcel sideways into the chute. The timing must be exact: too early and it misses the chute, too late and it hits the divider.

Higher speed means more parcels per hour — up to a point. The tilt window shrinks with speed, parcels slide differently, and a jam at one chute stops the whole loop. That is what the jam-risk gauge is telling you.

steps.title: Chutes, bags and cages
body: A chute is a slide with a destination. Parcels tumble down it into a bag, a cage or a roll container that is going to one city, one depot or one delivery route. When a bag is full, a light turns on and someone swaps it — or an automatic shuttle takes it away.
If a chute or its bag fills faster than it can be emptied, parcels back up and the sorter cannot discharge them; that chute becomes a bottleneck even though every carriage is still moving.

steps.title: Robots and shelves
body: The picking area is run by a fleet of low, orange AMRs. Each robot drives under a shelving pod, lifts it a few centimetres and carries it to a pack station; the picker takes the item and the robot returns the pod to its place.

With only ten robots the fleet cannot keep up with 55,000 parcels an hour, and the limit moves to induction. Add robots and the stream recovers; add too many and they queue for the same aisles. Real hubs tune the fleet against the day's order profile.

steps.title: Packing and outbound
body: At the pack bench a box is chosen, filled, taped, weighed and labelled. The label is the parcel's passport: it carries the destination, the service level and the route. A conveyor takes the sealed boxes to the outbound doors, where they are stacked into cages and rolled into trailers.

The outbound dock is the last queue. A trailer holds about 3,000 parcels, and a hub that can sort 40,000 an hour needs a trailer every few minutes — which is why the yard, not the building, often sets the pace at peak.

steps.title: Peak day
body: Press Peak burst. Arrivals jump by 70 %, but the sorter's speed and the fleet cannot jump with them: parcels queue on the induct belt, the backlog gauge climbs, and the only ways out are more hours, more chutes, more robots — or slowing the promise.

A hub is designed for average volume plus a safety margin. Peak day is the test of that margin: the sorter runs flat out, every chute is full, and the whole building becomes one long line of parcels waiting for their six minutes.

parts.name: Inbound trailer
parts.role: A floor-loaded semi-trailer backed onto the dock; loaders empty it through the rear doors.

parts.name: Dock door
parts.role: A sealed opening with a leveller and a shelter that keeps weather out of the hub.

parts.name: Telescopic conveyor
parts.role: A belt that extends deep into the trailer so loaders do not have to carry every parcel.

parts.name: Inbound belt
parts.role: Carries parcels from the trailer to the induct, where they are spaced one by one.

parts.name: Parcel
parts.role: A cardboard box with a barcode; its destination decides which chute it will take.

parts.name: Induct scanner
parts.role: Reads the barcode and measures the parcel; the control system assigns it a carriage.

parts.name: Parcel lift
parts.role: Lifts parcels from the unloading floor to the sorter deck.

parts.name: Sorter deck
parts.role: A steel mezzanine that carries the sorter loop above the ground-floor robots.

parts.name: Cross-belt sorter
parts.role: An endless loop of carriages; each short belt tips a parcel into one chute.

parts.name: Sorter carriage
parts.role: One link of the loop, with a belt, a motor and a controller that knows its parcel.

parts.name: Chute
parts.role: A slide from the sorter to a bag, cage or container for one destination.

parts.name: Bag cage
parts.role: A wheeled frame that collects the parcels for one route or depot.

parts.name: Sorter drive
parts.role: Linear motors and wheels that keep the loop moving at a constant speed.

parts.name: AMR robot
parts.role: An autonomous mobile robot that lifts a shelf pod and carries it to a pack station.

parts.name: Shelf pod
parts.role: A mobile shelving unit full of products; the robot lifts it off the floor.

parts.name: Storage rack
parts.role: Fixed shelving for slower-moving stock and bulk items.

parts.name: Pack station
parts.role: A bench where an order is boxed, taped, weighed and labelled.

parts.name: Taping arm
parts.role: A machine that folds and seals the box with tape.

parts.name: Outbound conveyor
parts.role: Carries sealed boxes from packing to the outbound dock.

parts.name: Outbound trailer
parts.role: A trailer being loaded with cages of sorted parcels.

parts.name: Tug and carts
parts.role: A small tractor that pulls cages between the hub and the yard.

facts.label: Distance a parcel travels
facts.value: a few hundred metres inside the hub

accuracy: Stage capacities are simple linear approximations: induction grows with the AMR fleet, the sorter with belt speed, and the chutes and outbound dock are fixed limits. The animation shows 40 carriages and 7 chutes slowed by roughly 20×; a real hub can run hundreds of chutes, several sorters and thousands of robots, with queueing, blocking and failures that this model does not capture.
